answers.answer: The argument is a plain `str`, so `escape()` takes the fast path at [__init__.py:39-40] — `if type(s) is str:` — and calls the module-level `_escape_inner(s)` (the C `_speedups` version if it imported, otherwise `_native`), wrapping the result in `Markup`. Only the five characters `& < > ' "` are replaced, so the result is `Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>')` — the parentheses, dot and semicolon are untouched.

A `Markup` is a `str` *subclass*, so `type(s) is str` is False and the fast path is skipped; `escape` falls to the `hasattr(s, "__html__")` branch [__init__.py:42-43] and returns `Markup(s.__html__())`. `Markup.__html__()` just returns `self`. Per the documented constructor [__init__.py:125-126], `Markup(obj)` itself also calls `__html__()` when the object has one, so `__html__()` ends up being invoked twice during that single `escape()` call — once by `escape`, once inside the `Markup(...)` constructor — both returning the same object, which is why the equality holds and no escaping occurs.

`EscapeFormatter.format_field` checks protocols in order; `User` defines `__html_format__`, so the first branch wins and it calls `user.__html_format__("link")`, which returns the `Markup('{1}').format(...)` value. The formatter then does `str(self.escape(rv))`; since `rv` is a `Markup`, `escape()` takes the `__html__` branch and returns it unchanged, so the anchor markup is spliced in verbatim rather than being escaped a second time.

`Markup` itself implements `__html_format__` [__init__.py:325-329], so `format_field` takes the *first* branch: it calls `comment.__html_format__("")`, which with an empty spec returns `self`, and the subsequent `escape()` is a no-op for a `Markup`. With `{comment:>40}` the same branch is taken but with a non-empty spec, and `Markup.__html_format__` raises `ValueError("Unsupported format specification for Markup.")`.

`Markup.__add__` accepts operands that are `str` or have `__html__`, escapes the operand with `self.escape(value)`, and returns a `Markup`. First addition: the right operand is a plain `str`, so it is escaped to `</p> & <script>oops</script>`. Second addition: the right operand is a `Markup`, so `escape()` passes it through via `__html__` and `</footer>` is appended verbatim. Final value: `Markup('<footer></p> & <script>oops</script></footer>')`.

Per [__init__.py:199-228], `striptags()` (1) finds and removes HTML comments `<!-- ... -->`, (2) removes all `<...>` tags, (3) collapses runs of whitespace to single spaces, and (4) *then* unescapes HTML entities; it returns a plain `str`, not a `Markup`. I can't give the exact returned string for this page: the question's `page` value isn't reproduced in the documentation I have, so the concrete result depends on the full template text. Note the ordering consequence: entity-escaped text such as `<script>` is unescaped only after tag removal, so it comes back as literal `<script>` in the returned string.

`Markup.format` uses `EscapeFormatter`, which escapes only the *substituted* field values, never the literal text of the template. `self.name` is a plain `str` with neither `__html_format__` nor `__html__`, so it goes through `super().format_field()` and then `escape()`, producing `Alice "The <b>Great</b>"`. The whole value is `Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')`. The quotes in `class="user"` live in the `Markup` literal, which is already marked safe by its constructor (which does no escaping), so they are left alone.

`escape()` knows only the `__html__` protocol — `__html_format__` is consulted exclusively by `EscapeFormatter` during `format()`/`format_map()`. Since `type(user) is not str` but `hasattr(user, "__html__")` is true, `escape` returns `Markup(user.__html__())`, i.e. the span markup from the previous question: `Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"')`. No format spec is involved and no re-escaping happens.

Using `type(s) is str` defeats proxy objects that override `__class__` to claim they are strings; with `isinstance()` such a proxy would take the "already a str" fast path and could slip through unescaped. With the identity check, only genuine `str` instances take the fast path. Everything else — including `str` subclasses such as `Markup` and oddities whose `str()` returns a subclass instance — falls through to the `__html__` check; if `__html__` exists its output is trusted, otherwise the object is converted with `str(s)` and then `_escape_inner`-escaped. The test suite explicitly covers proxy objects and `str` subclasses.

`Markup(object)` calls `object.__html__()` if that method exists and uses the returned string; otherwise it converts the object with `str()`. Crucially it performs **no escaping** — the content is marked safe as-is, which is the real trap: never pass untrusted input to the constructor (use `escape()`/`Markup.escape()` instead). `encoding` and `errors` are documented only as optional parameters for decoding byte strings; the documentation does not state what happens when bytes are passed with `encoding=None`, so I can't settle that case from the docs.

For `None`: `escape(None)` stringifies it and yields `Markup('None')`, whereas `escape_silent(None)` short-circuits and returns an empty `Markup('')`. For every other value `escape_silent` simply delegates to `escape`, so the behaviour is identical. `soft_str(s)` returns `s` unchanged when `isinstance(s, str)` — so a `Markup` stays a `Markup` and a plain `str` stays a `str` — and otherwise returns `str(s)`. The guarantee is type preservation: passing a `Markup` through `soft_str` before `escape` avoids double-escaping, unlike `str(markup)` which would make the already-escaped text get escaped again.

At import time `markupsafe/__init__.py` does `try: from ._speedups import _escape_inner / except ImportError: from ._native import _escape_inner`. The C extension is preferred; the pure-Python module is the fallback when the extension is missing (PyPy/Jython/GraalVM, compilation failure, `MARKUPSAFE_BUILD_FORCE_PURE=1`, ABI/import errors). Both expose the identical interface `_escape_inner(s: str, /) -> str` and identical functionality/API — only performance differs (the C version is substantially faster). The test suite's session-scoped `_mod` fixture runs the whole suite against both to enforce equivalence.

`striptags()` promises: unescape the markup, remove HTML comments and tags, and normalize whitespace, returning a plain `str`. Markup-looking text survives in two situations: (a) because unescaping happens *after* tag removal, entity-escaped sequences such as `<b>` reappear as literal `<b>` in the output; and (b) the result is a plain `str`, not `Markup`, so if you feed it back into a template it will be escaped again rather than being treated as safe. It is a text-extraction helper, not a sanitizer; its handling of newlines, ambiguous matches and whitespace collapsing was buggy enough to need fixes across 2.1.1–2.1.5.

`EscapeFormatter.format_field` dispatches in three steps: (1) if the value has `__html_format__`, call `value.__html_format__(format_spec)`; (2) else if the value has `__html__`, call `value.__html__()` — but only when no format spec was supplied; (3) otherwise fall back to `string.Formatter.format_field()`. In all cases the result is then passed through `str(self.escape(rv))`, which leaves `Markup`/`__html__` results untouched and escapes everything else. For a class that defines `__html__` but not `__html_format__` and is used with a non-empty format spec, step (2) raises a `ValueError` (the spec cannot be applied safely); the documentation describes this error but does not quote its exact message.
